triage.name: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
triage.reason: Newborn with a sentinel perinatal event, low Apgar scores and encephalopathy; diagnosis from delivery history, exam, blood gas and imaging, with therapeutic implications.

demographics: Occurs in about 1–2 per 1,000 live births in developed countries
More common in low-resource settings and where obstetric and neonatal care is limited

risk_factors.text: Sentinel perinatal event such as placental abruption, uterine rupture, cord prolapse or shoulder dystocia
Fetal bradycardia or non-reassuring fetal heart tracing before delivery
Low Apgar scores at 5 and 10 minutes
Need for resuscitation or assisted ventilation at birth

comorbidities: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

chief_complaints.text: My baby isn't breathing well on his own
The nurses say my baby is floppy and not waking up to feed

hpi.onset: At or shortly after birth, following a complicated delivery or a sentinel event during labor
hpi.duration: Present from the first minutes to hours of life; the encephalopathy evolves over the first 24–72 hours
hpi.progression: The newborn is depressed at birth with poor respiratory effort and low Apgar scores, then over the first day becomes increasingly lethargic, hypotonic and difficult to arouse; seizures often appear between 6 and 24 hours of life and tone may shift from floppy to stiff
hpi.quality: Depressed level of consciousness with abnormal tone and weak or absent reflexes
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; graded as mild, moderate or severe by the degree of encephalopathy
hpi.timing: Continuous from birth, with worsening over the first 1–3 days

associated_symptoms.text: Poor respiratory effort or apnea requiring resuscitation at birth
Low Apgar scores at 5 and 10 minutes
Weak or absent suck and Moro reflexes
Metabolic acidosis on the first blood gas
Feeding difficulty with poor oral intake
Abnormal movements such as cycling or lip smacking

pertinent_negatives: Fever or signs of sepsis before delivery
Family history of metabolic or neuromuscular disease
Hypoglycemia as the sole explanation for the encephalopathy

positives.text: Apnea or shallow breathing needing support

argues_against: Primary respiratory distress syndrome as the only cause

positives.text: Abnormal eye movements or fixed gaze

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm infants may show milder or atypical signs because the immature brain responds differently; seizures are often subtle and the encephalopathy can be missed.
The same hypoxic-ischemic injury after cardiac arrest or prolonged hypoxia in adults presents with coma, myoclonic jerks and a different workup; this profile describes the newborn presentation.

general.mild: Alert but jittery or irritable, startles easily, feeds with some coaxing
general.moderate: Lethargic and difficult to arouse, poor feeding, floppy or stiff limbs
general.severe: Stuporous or comatose, no spontaneous movement, requires ventilatory support
general.critical: Comatose and unresponsive, apnea requiring ventilation, seizures, hemodynamic instability

findings.maneuver: Observe the newborn's spontaneous activity and response to handling; attempt to arouse with gentle stimulation
findings.finding: Reduced level of consciousness, ranging from irritability to lethargy to coma

findings.maneuver: Assess limb and truncal tone by passive movement and observe posture
findings.finding: Floppy or stiff limbs with reduced resistance to passive movement

findings.maneuver: Place a finger or pacifier in the mouth and observe sucking; assess Moro and grasp reflexes
findings.finding: Weak or absent suck, Moro and grasp reflexes

findings.maneuver: Observe for abnormal movements such as cycling, lip smacking, eye deviation or subtle twitching
findings.finding: Clinical or electrographic seizures, often subtle

findings.maneuver: Observe eye position and movements; assess for fixed gaze or roving eyes
findings.finding: Abnormal eye movements or fixed gaze

findings.maneuver: Observe respiratory effort, rate and pattern; auscultate breath sounds
findings.finding: Shallow, irregular or absent respiratory effort requiring support

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure and assess perfusion
Assess limb movement and tone asymmetrically
Inspect skin for petechiae or rash

labs.caveat: Umbilical cord or first neonatal blood gas; a low pH with a base deficit supports a significant intrapartum hypoxic-ischemic event. A normal gas does not fully exclude the diagnosis.
A base deficit of about 12 mmol/L or more on the cord gas is one of the classic markers of a significant perinatal hypoxic-ischemic insult.
Respiratory component from hypoventilation or apnea; may be normal if the baby was vigorously resuscitated.
Elevated from anaerobic metabolism during the hypoxic-ischemic event; a high or rising lactate supports ongoing tissue hypoxia and correlates with severity.
Hypoglycemia is common after a perinatal insult and can itself worsen brain injury; it must be identified and corrected. A low glucose alone does not explain the full picture.
Acute kidney injury from the hypoxic-ischemic insult; creatinine may rise over the first days of life.
Elevated with hypoxic-ischemic injury to the liver; a very high AST/ALT with coagulopathy suggests multiorgan involvement.
Prolonged from hepatic injury and disseminated intravascular coagulation; important before any invasive procedure.
Thrombocytopenia from disseminated intravascular coagulation or liver injury.
Elevated with skeletal muscle injury from the hypoxic-ischemic event.
Hypocalcemia can accompany the perinatal insult and may lower the seizure threshold.
Ordered when an inborn error of metabolism is a consideration; a markedly elevated ammonia points away from hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy alone.
Mildly elevated in some cases; a marked pleocytosis or low glucose should raise concern for meningitis or encephalitis instead.

imaging.preferred_when: Bedside screening in the unstable newborn; useful for excluding hemorrhage or structural malformation

findings.text: May be normal in the first hours despite significant injury
Increased echogenicity of the basal ganglia or thalami
Loss of the normal resistance pattern on Doppler of the anterior cerebral artery
Germinal matrix or intraventricular hemorrhage (alternative diagnosis)

imaging.preferred_when: Days 3–7 of life, when diffusion changes are most conspicuous; the preferred study for confirming injury and prognosis

findings.text: Restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging in the basal ganglia, thalami and perirolandic cortex (deep gray matter pattern)
Restricted diffusion in the parasagittal watershed cortex and subcortical white matter (watershed pattern)
T2 hyperintensity and later T1 hyperintensity in the basal ganglia and thalami
Abnormal signal in the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Cortical ribboning with loss of the normal gray-white differentiation
Diffuse cerebral edema with effaced sulci and slit-like ventricles
Punctate white matter lesions or periventricular leukomalacia (more typical of preterm injury)
Usually normal or nonspecific in the newborn; not the study of choice
Diffuse cerebral edema with loss of gray-white differentiation
Patchy opacities or hyperinflation from meconium aspiration
Findings of respiratory distress syndrome in preterm infants

Marker of tissue hypoxia and severity
Hypoglycemia is common and worsens brain injury; must be corrected immediately
Electrolytes, renal function and acid-base status
Baseline counts and platelets; helps exclude infection
Liver enzymes and proteins to assess multiorgan hypoxic-ischemic injury
Coagulopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulation are common after a severe insult and matter before procedures
Bedside screen for hemorrhage or structural malformation in the unstable newborn
Confirms the pattern and extent of injury

supporting.why: Excludes meningitis or encephalitis when infection is a real concern
supporting.only_if: fever, maternal chorioamnionitis or an atypical course

Assesses myocardial injury after a severe perinatal insult

not_indicated.why: Radiation exposure and poor sensitivity in the newborn; MRI is preferred
No role in the evaluation of neonatal encephalopathy
Not part of the routine workup
Not part of the acute evaluation

decision_points: Confirm the diagnosis and grade the encephalopathy early, because therapeutic hypothermia is most effective when started within 6 hours of birth
Check and correct glucose, calcium and electrolytes before attributing all findings to hypoxic-ischemic injury
Exclude sepsis and meningitis when the presentation is atypical or there is maternal infection
Consider an inborn error of metabolism when there is no clear sentinel event or the course is unusual
MRI is best delayed to days 3–7 of life when diffusion changes are most conspicuous, unless another diagnosis must be excluded urgently

criteria.name: Clinical features supporting perinatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
criteria.summary: A sentinel perinatal event, low Apgar scores, need for resuscitation, and an early blood gas showing metabolic acidosis with a base deficit, together with encephalopathy (altered consciousness, abnormal tone and reflexes, and often seizures) in a term or near-term newborn.
items: Sentinel perinatal event or non-reassuring fetal heart tracing
Apgar score that stays low at 5 and 10 minutes
Need for resuscitation or assisted ventilation at birth
Metabolic acidosis with a base deficit on the cord or first neonatal gas
Encephalopathy with altered consciousness, abnormal tone and abnormal reflexes
Seizures, often within the first 24 hours

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: A depressed, floppy newborn with poor feeding, temperature instability and respiratory difficulty can look identical to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, and the two often coexist.
differential.trigger: Fever or temperature instability, maternal chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes, or a newborn who is unwell without a clear sentinel hypoxic event

history: Maternal fever, chorioamnionitis or prolonged rupture of membranes
No clear sentinel event such as abruption, cord prolapse or shoulder dystocia
Symptoms may evolve over hours rather than being present from the first minutes
exam: Signs of a focus such as omphalitis or a bulging fontanelle
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia with a left shift
CSF pleocytosis with low glucose and high protein if meningitis
imaging: Brain imaging is normal or nonspecific for infection

differential.name: Inborn error of metabolism
differential.why_considered: A lethargic, poorly feeding newborn with seizures, hypotonia and acidosis can mimic hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, especially when there is no clear perinatal event.
differential.trigger: No clear sentinel event, a worsening course after initial stabilization, or a family history of unexplained neonatal death or metabolic disease

history: Consanguinity or a family history of unexplained neonatal death
Deterioration after feeds or a symptom-free interval after birth
exam: Coarse features or dysmorphism in some disorders
Persistent or worsening encephalopathy despite supportive care
labs: Persistent metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap
Hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia or abnormal organic acids and acylcarnitine profile
Elevated lactate not explained by the perinatal event
imaging: Brain MRI may show symmetric white matter or basal ganglia changes that do not fit a hypoxic-ischemic pattern

differential.name: Neonatal stroke
differential.why_considered: A newborn with seizures and encephalopathy can have a perinatal arterial ischemic stroke rather than global hypoxic-ischemic injury.
differential.trigger: Focal seizures, a normal cord gas, or a normal Apgar score followed by seizures in the first days of life

history: Seizures may be the presenting feature with a relatively well newborn
Often no clear sentinel hypoxic event
May follow a difficult delivery or be associated with a prothrombotic state
exam: Focal seizures or focal neurologic signs
Usually preserved level of consciousness between seizures
labs: Cord gas often normal or only mildly abnormal
Thrombophilia workup may be abnormal in some cases
imaging: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging shows a focal arterial territory infarct, most often the middle cerebral artery
Cranial ultrasound may show focal echogenicity or asymmetry

differential.name: Intracranial hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: A depressed newborn with seizures, apnea and abnormal tone may have a germinal matrix, intraventricular or subdural hemorrhage rather than hypoxic-ischemic injury.
differential.trigger: Prematurity, traumatic delivery, a bulging fontanelle, a falling hematocrit, or focal neurologic findings

history: Preterm birth or traumatic delivery with instrumentation
Sudden deterioration with apnea or seizures
May have a normal cord gas
exam: Focal neurologic deficits or asymmetric tone
Pallor or shock if bleeding is significant
imaging: Cranial ultrasound shows germinal matrix or intraventricular hemorrhage
CT or MRI shows hemorrhage with mass effect or intraventricular blood

differential.name: Congenital neuromuscular disorder
differential.why_considered: A floppy newborn with poor respiratory effort and weak suck can resemble hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, but the encephalopathy and perinatal event are absent.

exam: Alert and responsive despite severe hypotonia
Weak cry, weak suck and preserved extraocular movements
labs: Elevated creatine kinase in some myopathies
Normal blood gas or only mild respiratory acidosis
imaging: Muscle biopsy or genetic testing confirms the diagnosis

differential.name: Neonatal seizure disorder
differential.why_considered: Seizures in a newborn can be caused by a primary epilepsy syndrome or a structural brain malformation rather than hypoxic-ischemic injury.

history: Family history of neonatal seizures or epilepsy
Seizures may be the only abnormality with a normal perinatal history
exam: Normal tone and alertness between seizures
labs: Normal blood gas, lactate and metabolic studies
Genetic testing may identify a channelopathy
imaging: Brain MRI may show a structural malformation or be normal
EEG shows a characteristic pattern for the syndrome

severity.mild: Alert but irritable or jittery, mild hypotonia, weak suck, no seizures; resolves over days with supportive care
severity.moderate: Lethargic and difficult to arouse, significant hypotonia or hypertonia, weak or absent reflexes, seizures common; requires therapeutic hypothermia and intensive monitoring
severity.severe: Stuporous or comatose, no spontaneous movement, apnea requiring ventilation, frequent seizures, multiorgan involvement; high risk of death or major neurodevelopmental disability
severity.critical: Comatose and unresponsive, persistent apnea requiring ventilation, refractory seizures, hemodynamic instability and multiorgan failure; may be fatal despite maximal support

red_flags.finding: Apnea or need for assisted ventilation at birth
red_flags.meaning: Severe brainstem involvement and a marker of a significant hypoxic-ischemic insult
Moderate to severe encephalopathy; requires urgent EEG monitoring and treatment

red_flags.finding: Cord or first blood gas pH below 7.0 with a base deficit of 12 mmol/L or more
red_flags.meaning: Confirms a significant intrapartum hypoxic-ischemic event and supports therapeutic hypothermia
Can worsen brain injury and must be corrected immediately

red_flags.finding: Multiorgan failure with oliguria, elevated liver enzymes or coagulopathy
red_flags.meaning: Severe global hypoxic-ischemic injury with a poor prognosis

red_flags.finding: Bulging fontanelle or focal neurologic deficit
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an alternative diagnosis such as intracranial hemorrhage or stroke

complications.name: Neonatal seizures
clues: Subtle movements such as cycling, lip smacking or eye deviation

complications.name: Cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure
Acute kidney injury
clues: Rising creatinine over the first days of life

complications.name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
clues: Severe hypoxemia out of proportion to lung disease

complications.name: Neurodevelopmental disability
clues: Cerebral palsy with spasticity or dystonia

special_populations.differences: Preterm infants may show milder or atypical signs because the immature brain responds differently; seizures are often subtle and the encephalopathy can be missed. Therapeutic hypothermia is generally reserved for term and near-term infants.
The same hypoxic-ischemic injury after cardiac arrest or prolonged hypoxia in adults presents with coma, myoclonic jerks and a different workup; this profile describes the newborn presentation.

key_questions.question: How was the delivery — was there any problem during labor or at birth?
key_questions.looking_for: A sentinel perinatal event such as placental abruption, uterine rupture, cord prolapse, shoulder dystocia or prolonged obstructed labor

key_questions.question: Did the baby need help breathing or resuscitation right after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Need for assisted ventilation or resuscitation, indicating a significant hypoxic-ischemic insult at birth

key_questions.question: What were the Apgar scores, and did they stay low at 5 and 10 minutes?
key_questions.looking_for: Apgar scores that remain low at 5 and 10 minutes, a classic marker of perinatal asphyxia

key_questions.question: Was the fetal heart tracing abnormal before delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Fetal bradycardia or non-reassuring fetal heart tracing suggesting intrapartum hypoxia

key_questions.question: Was the amniotic fluid stained with meconium?
key_questions.looking_for: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid, which supports a hypoxic event and raises concern for meconium aspiration

key_questions.question: How is the baby feeding and waking up for feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, weak suck and difficulty arousing, reflecting encephalopathy

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any seizures or unusual movements?
key_questions.looking_for: Subtle seizures such as cycling, lip smacking, eye deviation or apnea, often within the first 24 hours

key_questions.question: Has the baby's temperature been stable?
key_questions.looking_for: Temperature instability or hypothermia, common after a perinatal insult

key_questions.question: Was there any maternal fever, infection or prolonged rupture of membranes?
key_questions.looking_for: Chorioamnionitis or intrauterine infection, which can mimic or coexist with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy

key_questions.question: How many weeks pregnant were you when you delivered?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm birth, which alters the presentation and eligibility for therapeutic hypothermia

key_questions.question: Was this a multiple gestation or was the baby growth-restricted?
key_questions.looking_for: Twins or fetal growth restriction, which increase the risk of a perinatal hypoxic event

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of metabolic disease, neuromuscular disease or unexplained neonatal death?
key_questions.looking_for: A family history that raises concern for an inborn error of metabolism or congenital neuromuscular disorder

key_questions.question: Did the baby have a blood gas drawn, and what did it show?
key_questions.looking_for: Metabolic acidosis with a base deficit on the cord or first neonatal gas, supporting a significant hypoxic-ischemic event

key_questions.question: Has the baby's blood sugar been checked?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypoglycemia, which is common after a perinatal insult and can worsen brain injury

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any fever, rash or signs of infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever, petechiae or rash suggesting sepsis or congenital infection rather than hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy alone

accepted_names: Neonatal encephalopathy due to perinatal asphyxia
reasoning_points: A sentinel perinatal event such as placental abruption, uterine rupture, cord prolapse or shoulder dystocia
Low Apgar scores that remain low at 5 and 10 minutes with a need for resuscitation or assisted ventilation at birth
Metabolic acidosis with a base deficit on the cord or first neonatal blood gas
Encephalopathy with altered consciousness, abnormal tone and weak or absent primitive reflexes
Seizures, often subtle and appearing within the first 24 hours of life
Exclusion of look-alikes such as neonatal sepsis, inborn error of metabolism, neonatal stroke and intracranial hemorrhage
MRI showing a characteristic pattern of injury in the basal ganglia, thalami, perirolandic cortex or watershed regions
Recognition that therapeutic hypothermia is most effective when started within 6 hours of birth

easy: Term newborn with a clear sentinel event such as placental abruption or cord prolapse
Low Apgar scores at 5 and 10 minutes with a need for resuscitation
Cord gas showing metabolic acidosis with a base deficit
Lethargic, floppy baby with poor feeding and weak reflexes
Seizures within the first 24 hours of life
medium: No clear sentinel event but a non-reassuring fetal heart tracing and low Apgar scores
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid with respiratory distress and encephalopathy
Mild encephalopathy with irritability and jitteriness rather than lethargy
Preterm infant with subtle seizures and atypical neurologic signs
Coexisting maternal chorioamnionitis making sepsis a strong alternative
hard: No clear perinatal event and a worsening course suggesting an inborn error of metabolism
Newborn with focal seizures and a normal cord gas suggesting neonatal stroke
Premature infant with a bulging fontanelle and falling hematocrit suggesting intracranial hemorrhage
Floppy infant who is alert and responsive with a normal blood gas suggesting a congenital neuromuscular disorder
Mild encephalopathy that is missed because the baby initially feeds and appears well
